cards.front: In Git, what is a commit?
cards.back: A saved snapshot of your project at one moment, with a message describing what changed.

cards.front: Download the repository at https://github.com/acme/etl.git into a folder named pipeline instead of the default name
cards.back: `git clone https://github.com/acme/etl.git pipeline`

cards.front: Show the state of your repository's files as a compact list, one line per file
cards.back: `git status -s`

cards.front: In Git, what is the working directory?
cards.back: The actual files in your project folder that you see and edit, including changes not yet committed.

cards.front: In Git, what is a repository?
cards.back: A project folder whose history Git tracks; the history itself lives in a hidden `.git` folder inside it.

cards.front: Stage the changes in `etl.py` so they go into the next commit
cards.back: `git add etl.py`

cards.front: Stage every change in the current directory and below for the next commit
cards.back: `git add .`

cards.front: Why does Git have a staging area between your files and a commit?
cards.back: So you choose exactly which changes go into the next commit, not everything you edited.

cards.front: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
cards.back: Git is the tool that tracks history; GitHub is a website that stores Git repositories online for sharing.

cards.front: What is version control?
cards.back: A system that records every change to your files, so you can see history and go back to older versions.

cards.front: Show the commit history with one short line per commit
cards.back: `git log --oneline`

cards.front: Show the list of commits, newest first, with author, date and message
cards.back: `git log`

cards.front: Turn the current folder into a new, empty Git repository
cards.back: `git init`

cards.front: Create a new folder named pipeline and make it an empty Git repository in one step
cards.back: `git init pipeline`

cards.front: What is Git?
cards.back: A version control tool that runs on your own computer; it works without internet or any website.

cards.front: See which files in your repository are modified, staged or untracked
cards.back: `git status`

cards.front: Does a Git commit record a list of changes, or a snapshot of the project?
cards.back: A snapshot of all tracked files; the diffs Git shows are computed by comparing two snapshots.

cards.front: Save the staged changes as a commit with the message `Add ETL script`, without opening an editor
cards.back: `git commit -m "Add ETL script"`

cards.front: What path does a change take from your editor into a commit?
cards.back: Edited in the working directory, staged with `git add`, then recorded with `git commit`.Working directoryStaging areagit addCommit historygit commit

cards.front: You run `git add app.py`, edit `app.py` again, then run `git commit`. Which version gets committed?
cards.back: The version from when you ran `git add`; the later edit stays uncommitted until you add it again.
